title: Grammar: Give or follow a short instruction: the imperative
subtitle: A2 · Unit 11: Solve a practical problem politely

steps.title: Give or follow a short instruction: the imperative
steps.body: A practical request usually has three parts: state the problem, ask for one action and confirm what happens next. French uses the imperative for a direct instruction and the conditional of pouvoir or vouloir to make many requests sound more courteous.

steps.title: These short messages reuse the lesson's document vocabulary and model one useful instruction.
rows: Il n'y a pas de copie recto verso.

steps.title: The imperative has no written subject pronoun. Use vous for an unfamiliar service contact or a plural group. With a regular -er verb, the familiar tu form drops final -s: tu coches → coche.
rows: Ne cochez pas la mauvaise case.

steps.title: Give or follow a short instruction: the imperative
steps.body:
• For an affirmative instruction, use the tu, nous or vous verb form without the subject: coche; cochons; cochez.
• For a negative instruction, place ne (or n' before a vowel sound) before the verb and pas after it: ne cochez pas; n'appuyez pas.
• Use tu only when the relationship is familiar. Use vous with an unfamiliar customer-service contact or when speaking to several people.
• For regular -er verbs, the tu imperative drops final -s: tu coches → coche. Other verbs do not all follow this pattern: tu choisis → choisis.
• Keep an instruction short and limited to the next action. For a request to another person, the conditional form may be more suitable.

steps.prompt: Choose the polite instruction for an unfamiliar service contact.
steps.explain: Use the vous imperative for an unfamiliar service contact.

options: Ne appuyez pas sur le bouton.
steps.explain: Before a vowel sound, ne shortens to n'; pas follows the verb.

steps.prompt: What happens to a regular -er verb in the familiar tu imperative?
options: The subject tu stays: tu coche.
The verb moves after the object.
steps.explain: The familiar imperative of a regular -er verb drops the final -s.
